explanation: What looks like one yellow flower is really a tight cluster of many tiny florets, and each floret makes a single seed with its own parachute.

claims.text: Dandelion seed heads, called clocks, release seeds that drift on the wind under parachute-like tufts.
Daisies, poppies and buttercups do not form fluffy seed clocks of parachuted seeds.
A dandelion flower head is a cluster of many small florets.
Each dandelion floret produces a single seed with its own parachute.

evidence.restatement: A dandelion's round seed head, the clock, releases seeds that float off on parachute-like tufts (the pappus).
Daisies, poppies and buttercups set seed without parachute tufts and never form a fluffy seed clock.
A dandelion flower head is a composite of many small florets.
Each floret ripens into one single-seeded fruit topped by its own pappus parachute.
A dandelion seed head (the 'clock') releases seeds that float away on parachute-like tufts.
The lawn daisy, poppies and buttercups do not make fluffy, parachuted seed clocks.

claimResults.note: True of the plants these names normally mean. Some other daisy-family plants, such as asters and fleabanes, do have fluffy seeds (see the issue).

evidence.restatement: A dandelion 'flower' is a head of many small florets.
Each dandelion floret becomes one single-seeded fruit topped by a parachute-like tuft.

issues.note: 'Clock' is a mainly British name for the seed head. The stem describes it fully (fluffy, drifting, parachutes), so players elsewhere can still reach dandelion.

'Daisy' is a loose label: asters and fleabanes are called daisies and do have parachuted seeds, though the lawn daisy and ox-eye do not. Not a second answer, because dandelion is the only option with a famous seed 'clock'.

stem: Which plant's fluffy 'clock' of seeds drifts away on the wind, each seed hanging from a tiny parachute?
